passage: In my first month of college, the hostel's first-year group chat became a place where seniors posted my photos with captions about my 'village English' and my oiled hair. Every day, a new one. When I finally wrote 'please stop', a senior replied, 'Relax, it's just ragging, it's fun, everyone goes through it.' I believed that for a while. I told myself I was too sensitive. I stopped eating in the mess. Then Himani, my roommate, read the chat over my shoulder and said, 'Sarita, this isn't fun. They're humiliating you every day.' Hearing it named plainly was like breathing again. She walked with me to the warden that same evening. The warden listened, said none of it was my fault, and called the anti-ragging committee before we left the office. It stopped within a week.

qa.q: What did the senior reply when Sarita wrote 'please stop'?
qa.a: The senior replied, 'Relax, it's just ragging, it's fun, everyone goes through it.'

qa.q: Why did Sarita start to believe that the problem was being too sensitive?
qa.a: The label 'just ragging' made the daily mockery sound normal, so Sarita's real hurt began to look like the problem instead of what the seniors were doing.

qa.q: What choice by Himani changed things, and why?
qa.a: Himani named it plainly as humiliation and walked Sarita to the warden that same evening, which turned private pain into something adults could act on.

qa.q: How did the warden respond, and why did it matter to Sarita?
qa.a: The warden listened, said none of it was Sarita's fault and called the anti-ragging committee at once, which showed that Sarita was believed and protected.

grounding: Shows a first-year student mocked daily in a group chat who is told it is only ragging, until a roommate names it plainly and the warden acts the same evening.

passage:
Counsellor's note, college counselling cell, Monday
Neelam, first-year B.Sc., came in at 4 p.m. and showed me her phone. For three weeks her class group chat has been posting edited pictures of her with an animal's face, and voice notes copying her stammer. When she complained, the group admin wrote, 'It's just fun, bro. Don't be so serious.' She said to me, 'Maybe I can't take a joke.' Her hands shook while she scrolled. I told her plainly that this is mockery, not fun, that it is not her fault, and that she was right to come. With her permission I took screenshots and reported it to the anti-ragging committee and the head of department before six this evening. I've arranged for a senior mentor to sit with her in class, and her parents know. I'll see her again tomorrow at lunch.
Swati

qa.q: What did the group admin write when Neelam complained?
qa.a: The admin wrote, 'It's just fun, bro. Don't be so serious.'

qa.q: Why did Neelam say 'Maybe I can't take a joke'?
qa.a: Being told it was 'just fun' made Neelam doubt her own hurt, so she blamed herself instead of the people mocking her.

qa.q: Which of Swati's steps matters most, and why?
qa.a: Calling it mockery and saying it wasn't Neelam's fault gives her distress its real name, and reporting it the same day makes sure it actually stops.

qa.q: How might the group admin see the chat differently from Neelam?
qa.a: The admin sees harmless fun from the outside, while for Neelam each edited picture and voice note has meant three weeks of dread and shaking hands.

grounding: Shows a counsellor's note on a student mocked in a class group chat and told it was just fun, who names it plainly and reports it the same day.

passage:
Wednesday night
Today the seniors' group posted my photo again, the one from orientation where I tripped, with 'Miss Circus' written over it. Forty-two laughing reactions. When I asked one of them to take it down, she said, 'It's just ragging, yaar. It's how we bond.' It doesn't feel like bonding. It feels like I can't walk into the canteen. I cried in the washroom before lab.
Vikas saw my face and asked. I showed him. He didn't say 'ignore it'. He said, 'That's bullying, Sunaina. Calling it ragging doesn't make it okay.' He came with me to the warden's office after lab. Warden ma'am read every post, said it was not my fault, and phoned the anti-ragging committee right there. The photo was gone by 9 p.m.
I'm still shaky. But someone called it by its real name.

qa.a: The photo got forty-two laughing reactions.

qa.q: What does 'It doesn't feel like bonding' show about how Sunaina feels?
qa.a: It shows that Sunaina's real experience, dreading the canteen and crying before lab, doesn't match the friendly label, which was trying to erase that hurt.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that made a difference?
qa.a: Vikas named it plainly as bullying instead of saying 'ignore it', then went with Sunaina to the warden that same afternoon, so an adult could act.

qa.a: Hearing it was not Sunaina's fault and seeing the photo gone by 9 p.m. showed that Sunaina was believed, even though the shakiness remained 🤍.

passage:
The local bus from Kheri to the polytechnic in Sirsa rattled over every pothole, and Jasleen kept her phone face down on her knee. Rajni reached over and turned it up. The class group again: Jasleen's photo from the field visit, mud on her chappals, captioned 'Village Queen arrives', with forty laughing reactions under it.
'Arre, it's just masti,' Rajni said. 'They tease everyone in first year.'
Jasleen looked out at the mustard fields. 'You say masti, so I'm supposed to smile. I've eaten lunch behind the workshop for a week so they can't see me.'
Rajni's thumb stopped over the screen. One of the forty reactions was hers.
'They're mocking you,' she said slowly, 'and it's hurting you.'
She took back her reaction, then typed in the group: 'Not funny. Stop.'

qa.a: Jasleen has eaten lunch behind the workshop for a week so they can't see her.

qa.q: What does Jasleen's face-down phone suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she dreads seeing the group; she feels ashamed and wants to hide from the jokes, not laugh along with them.

qa.q: Which choice of Rajni's changed things on the bus, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Rajni stopped calling it masti, said plainly that they were mocking Jasleen and it was hurting her, then took back her reaction and posted 'Not funny. Stop.'; naming it let Jasleen's hurt count.

qa.q: What might Rajni feel on noticing that one of the forty reactions was her own?
qa.a: Rajni probably feels a jolt of guilt, realising she had been part of the crowd that made the joke look harmless while Jasleen was eating alone.

grounding: A student whose mockery in the class group is waved off as masti tells a friend what it really costs her, and the friend names it plainly.

passage: Tanvir, you've gone quiet since you told me about that group chat, and I'm not letting it pass with a joke. Let your Usha Nani tell you something first. My first month in the women's hostel in Pune, the seniors pinned a drawing of me on the mess notice board every morning. My plaits, my village sari, a cow beside me. Everyone laughed. When I cried, they said, 'It's only ragging, yaar. Fun. Everyone goes through it.' I believed my hurt was the silly thing, not what they did. Then my roommate Farzana took me to the warden, Mrs Pinto. She looked at the drawings and said, 'This is not fun. This is humiliation, and it stops today.' Those plain words gave me my breath back. So now, beta, after dinner, you and I are calling your warden together, and then your mother.

qa.a: They pinned it on the mess notice board every morning.

passage: It was the night before Samir's first semester exam, and the paying-guest house in Indore was loud with other boys cramming. His phone buzzed again: the batch group chat, another voice note mimicking his stammer, this one set to music. Forty-two laughing reactions. He sat on his bed with the chemistry book open and read the same line five times. Hemant, from the next room, leaned in. 'Bro, ignore it. It's just ragging. Fun. They do it to everyone.' 'Everyone gets a song about their stammer?' Samir said. 'It's not fun. It's mocking me, every day, in front of the whole batch.' Hemant went quiet, then sat down beside him. 'Okay. Then we tell someone tonight.' Samir called his faculty mentor with Hemant beside him. The mentor listened, asked him to save every message, and said the anti-ragging committee would have it before the first exam.

qa.q: How many laughing reactions did the voice note get?
qa.a: The voice note got forty-two laughing reactions.

qa.q: Why did Samir read the same line five times?
qa.a: He was hurt and humiliated by the daily mockery, and the pain made it impossible to focus the night before his exam.

qa.q: What changed when Samir named it plainly?
qa.a: Calling it mocking instead of fun made Hemant take it seriously, and together they told the faculty mentor that night.

qa.q: How does Hemant see it once Samir speaks?
qa.a: Hemant stops calling it fun, realises it is targeted mockery, and stays beside Samir while he reports it.

passage: The class group chat at the Chandigarh college had a new sticker: Gurleen's face from the orientation photo, cropped onto a cartoon of a village aunty with a milk can. It was the sixth one this month, and twenty people had replied with laughing faces. In the canteen, Divyansh slid his tray next to hers. 'Don't take it so seriously. It's college fun. Everyone gets ragged in first year.' Gurleen put down her spoon. 'Fun is when everyone's laughing. I'm not. This is people mocking me every week because of where I'm from.' Divyansh looked at his dal. 'I didn't make them.' 'You reacted to four.' He didn't answer. That afternoon Gurleen took screenshots of every sticker to her class mentor, Dr Bedi, who read them in silence and said, 'Thank you for bringing these. This is harassment, and it goes to the committee today.' That evening she called her mother and told her everything.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen put down her spoon when Divyansh called it college fun?
qa.a: She felt hurt and angry that her distress was being brushed off, and she wanted the mockery named for what it was.

qa.a: She named it plainly to Divyansh, took screenshots of every sticker to Dr Bedi, and called her mother that evening.

qa.a: Calling it fun lets Divyansh avoid feeling responsible for the four reactions he added and for the hurt it causes Gurleen.

“Chinmay, your phone's buzzing again.”
“I know, Tanuja.” He turned it face down on the canteen table.
“Is it the batch group? Oh, the voice-note thing.” She laughed, then stopped. “Come on, it's only ragging. Everyone gets a nickname in first year.”

passage:
Looking back, the worst part was not the stickers. It was the word everyone used for them.
In my second semester, the hostel group started pasting my face onto cartoon rats. Every morning there would be a new one. I, Rafiq, became “Ratfiq” to thirty people.
When I told Vasudha, my lab partner, she shrugged. “It's banter. They do it to everyone they like.” I nodded, because nodding was easier. For weeks I told myself the same thing: banter, harmless, a sign of being liked.
But I was eating dinner in my room to avoid the mess. I had muted the group and still checked it at 2 a.m.
One evening I wrote the true sentence in my notes app: they are humiliating me and I dread every morning. Seeing it written down, I finally went to the student counsellor, and I stopped calling it banter.

qa.q: What did the hostel group paste the narrator's face onto?
qa.a: They pasted Rafiq's face onto cartoon rats, and a new one appeared every morning.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq keep repeating the word banter for weeks?
qa.a: Rafiq felt ashamed and wanted to fit in, so the friendly word was a comfort; admitting humiliation felt harder than nodding along.

qa.q: What helped Rafiq move from confusion to action?
qa.a: Writing one plain, true sentence about the humiliation and dread; it made the harm clear enough to take to the student counsellor.

qa.q: How might Vasudha see the stickers differently if she had known about the dinners in the room and the 2 a.m. checking?
qa.a: She might stop calling it banter and see that Rafiq was hurting and needed support, not a shrug.

grounding: The passage shows repeated group-chat mockery being relabelled as banter, and the receiver finally naming the distress plainly.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday.
Sahil (first-year, B.Com) came in at 11 a.m. and sat without speaking for almost a minute. He had screenshots ready on his phone. In the section group, several classmates post edited photos of him with captions about his weight, most nights for the past month.
He said he had raised it with Yogesh, the class representative, who told him it was "just ragging, a tradition, nothing personal." Sahil repeated that phrase twice, as if checking whether he was allowed to be upset.
I told him plainly that what he described is repeated mocking, that his distress makes sense, and that it is not his fault.
Next steps: with his consent I forwarded the screenshots to the anti-ragging committee the same afternoon, and the convenor called him before 5 p.m. I have asked to meet Yogesh tomorrow about how complaints are handled. Follow-up with Sahil on Monday.

qa.a: Yogesh, the class representative, told him it was “just ragging, a tradition, nothing personal.”

qa.q: Why did Sahil repeat Yogesh's phrase twice?
qa.a: He seemed unsure and ashamed, as if checking whether he was allowed to feel hurt when the mocking had been called a tradition.

qa.q: Which of the counsellor's steps helped most, and what could come next?
qa.a: The counsellor named the behaviour as repeated mocking, told Sahil it was not his fault and passed the screenshots to the committee the same day; next, the meeting with Yogesh can change how complaints are handled.

passage:
Tuesday night, hostel
The second-year group chat did it again today. Someone posted a photo of my cracked sandals with "Village fashion week". Then a voice note copying the way I say "hospital". Forty laughing replies. When I didn't react, a senior messaged me privately: "Relax, it's just ragging. Fun. Everyone goes through it."
Fun. I sat on my bed and couldn't eat dinner. My chest has felt tight since Sunday. I've stopped going to the common room.
So let me write it the plain way, without their words. They are mocking me, in public, every day, and it hurts.
After dinner I told Amandeep. Amandeep didn't say "relax". We went together to the warden's office straight away. The warden read the messages, said, "This is harassment, not fun," and called the anti-ragging committee head while we sat there. There's a meeting tomorrow at nine.
Saurabh

qa.a: The senior said, "Relax, it's just ragging. Fun."

qa.a: Saurabh feels hurt and humiliated, chest tight and unable to eat, and calling it fun dismisses that pain as if it isn't real.

qa.a: Amandeep was probably upset and protective, taking it seriously at once and going with Saurabh to the warden.

passage:
July in Cape Town meant rain on the residence windows and heaters that clicked all night. For three weeks the first-year group chat had been doing the same thing to Alejandro: voice notes imitating his accent, a photo of him asleep in the library captioned "the tourist". When he muted the chat, a senior messaged him: "Relax, it's just first-year fun. Everyone gets it."
That evening he knocked on Zanele's door. She was the residence mentor, and she put the kettle on while he scrolled through the messages for her, his voice flat.
"They say it's just fun."
Zanele read for a long while. "This is you being mocked, over and over, in front of eighty people. You're allowed to call it that." She wrote down the dates. "I'm taking this to the residence head tonight, and I'll tell you tomorrow morning what happens next."

qa.a: Zanele read the messages, named them plainly as repeated mocking, wrote down the dates, and took it to the residence head that same night, promising to update him in the morning.

qa.a: The senior probably sees it as ordinary first-year teasing that everyone goes through, which misses that for Alejandro it has been three weeks of being laughed at in front of eighty people.
